paragraphs: Related prediction tasks can benefit from learning a common feature representation. This paper studies how to discover that shared structure while training the tasks together. It begins with alternating structure optimization, or ASO, and develops an improved formulation called iASO. The central challenge is that this formulation is nonconvex, making its optimization difficult.

The authors construct a convex relaxation of iASO. Although this changes the optimization problem into a more tractable mathematical form, its complicated constraints still make direct application unsuitable for large datasets. They therefore introduce cASO, an alternating optimization algorithm designed to solve the relaxation efficiently, and prove that it converges to a global optimum of that relaxed problem.

A separate theoretical condition establishes when cASO also recovers a globally optimal solution of the original iASO formulation. That distinction matters: solving the relaxation globally does not automatically settle the original problem. Experiments on several benchmark datasets support the theoretical analysis, connecting the proposed formulation and algorithm to practical multitask learning.
icml-2009-a-convex-formulation-for-learn.tldr: The paper develops an efficient algorithm for a convex relaxation of shared multitask learning, with conditional guarantees for the original nonconvex formulation.

paragraphs: A meaningful cluster may involve only some objects and some features. In microarray analysis, for example, a subset of genes may behave cohesively only under particular conditions. Treating every feature as equally relevant can hide this pattern among many uninformative measurements. Different clusters may also depend on different subsets of features.

The paper introduces Robust Overlapping Co-clustering, or ROCC, to address this setting. Co-clustering searches for groups of objects together with the features that make those groups coherent. ROCC targets dense groups in large, noisy datasets and allows them to occur in arbitrary positions. It also permits overlap, so discovered groups need not form a mutually exclusive partition.

The contribution is a scalable framework that brings these requirements together. Its flexibility matters because the relevant objects and relevant features are both part of what must be discovered. The abstract presents ROCC as suitable for multiple practical applications, emphasizing efficient discovery of local structure amid noise rather than requiring one feature space to explain every cluster.
icml-2009-a-scalable-framework-for-disco.tldr: ROCC searches large, noisy datasets for dense, potentially overlapping groups of objects and their relevant features.

paragraphs: An observation can contain several hidden features at once, and the same feature can recur across observations. The Indian Buffet Process provides a nonparametric prior for representing which features are present. The paper addresses the computational difficulty of inferring these hidden feature assignments when the number of observations becomes large.

Existing Gibbs sampling approaches present a tradeoff. The collapsed sampler has a running time that grows cubically with the number of observations. The uncollapsed sampler scales linearly, but often mixes slowly, meaning it can take time to move effectively through the possibilities being considered. Thus, cheaper computation alone does not resolve the inference problem.

The authors introduce a collapsed Gibbs sampler with linear running time for conjugate models. This retains the collapsed approach while changing its dependence on dataset size from cubic to linear in the stated setting. They demonstrate its effectiveness on several large real-world datasets. The contribution is therefore an inference improvement for an established hidden-feature model, with the linear-time claim specifically tied to conjugate models.
icml-2009-accelerated-sampling-for-the-i.tldr: A new collapsed Gibbs sampler makes Indian Buffet Process inference scale linearly with observation count for conjugate models.

paragraphs: Words tend to recur within a document: after a word appears once, another occurrence becomes more likely. This burstiness is a property of language that the paper argues existing topic models fail to capture adequately. The issue concerns how repeated observations are modeled, even when a topic model otherwise works well for its applications.

The authors introduce a topic model using Dirichlet compound multinomial distributions to represent this behavior. These distributions provide a way to account for concentrated repetition within a document. The approach makes burstiness part of the probabilistic model, so the model can reflect the tendency for occurrences to arrive in groups.

On both text and non-text datasets, the proposed model obtains better held-out likelihood than standard latent Dirichlet allocation. This indicates a better probabilistic fit to unseen data in those evaluations; it is not a claim about every possible downstream task. The authors also state that the extension can be incorporated straightforwardly into topic models more complex than LDA, giving the modeling idea a broader potential role.
icml-2009-accounting-for-burstiness-in-t.tldr: Modeling repeated occurrences with Dirichlet compound multinomial distributions improves held-out likelihood over standard LDA on the evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Filtering estimates the evolving state of a system from uncertain observations. This paper considers nonlinear stochastic dynamical systems modeled with Gaussian processes. Its focus is on computing the expected state and its covariance, which describe the estimate and the uncertainty associated with it during the filtering process.

The proposed filter derives analytic expressions for these quantities in both the prediction step and the filtering step. Prediction carries the estimate forward, while filtering incorporates observations. The expressions for the filtering step exploit an additional Gaussian assumption. Within this formulation, the method requires no further approximations and specifically avoids approximating the moments through samples.

The significance is that the required uncertainty summaries can be calculated analytically under the stated modeling assumptions. This should not be read as an unrestricted claim of exact inference for every nonlinear system. The paper compares the method with several Gaussian filters, including the extended Kalman filter, unscented Kalman filter, and Gaussian-process unscented Kalman filter, placing its analytic approach alongside established alternatives.
icml-2009-analytic-moment-based-gaussian.tldr: The paper derives analytic filtering moments for Gaussian-process dynamical models, using an additional Gaussian assumption in the filtering step.

paragraphs: Boosting builds a predictor by progressively adding useful components. This paper develops generalizations of AdaBoost and related gradient-based coordinate descent methods that also penalize the size or structure of the learned predictor. The aim is to make sparsity part of the learning procedure itself.

The resulting algorithms combine forward feature induction with back-pruning through regularization. They can add features while also removing previously included ones, and they provide an automatic criterion for stopping feature induction. The authors study penalties based on the l1, l2, and infinity norms, then construct mixed-norm penalties from these ingredients.

The mixed norms support structural sparsity: the organization of which parameters remain active matters, beyond simply reducing their total number. The abstract identifies multiclass prediction and related tasks as useful settings for this property. Empirical results demonstrate that the approach can produce models that are both accurate and structurally sparse. The contribution connects feature selection, pruning, and stopping decisions within one family of regularized coordinate descent algorithms.
icml-2009-boosting-with-structural-spars.tldr: Regularized boosting algorithms combine feature addition, pruning, and automatic stopping to learn accurate models with structural sparsity.

paragraphs: Label ranking asks a model to order a fixed collection of labels for each input. The prediction is a complete ranking rather than one selected category or one numerical value. Learning therefore has to account for how labels relate to one another within the order assigned to an instance.

The paper adapts two familiar learning approaches to this output type: instance-based learning and decision tree induction. Both have been widely used for classification and regression. Extending them to rankings broadens the available methods for a problem in which the output contains several coordinated ordering decisions.

The shared ingredient is a procedure that locally estimates predictive probability models over label rankings. This supplies a common probabilistic basis for the two otherwise different approaches. Local estimation connects the ranking prediction to the relevant part of the input data, while the probability model represents possible orders. The authors present the resulting methods as complementing and improving existing approaches, with the main contribution being this adaptation of established learners through a unified ranking-model estimation procedure.
icml-2009-decision-tree-and-instance-bas.tldr: The paper extends decision trees and instance-based learning to label ranking using local probability models over complete label orders.

paragraphs: Transfer learning seeks to reuse knowledge when training and test settings differ. This paper studies a particularly substantial change: the target domain is described using different predicates, or kinds of relations, from the source domain. The authors call this deep transfer, distinguishing it from a distribution change within the same domain.

Their approach uses a form of second-order Markov logic to discover structural regularities. Learned formulas contain variables standing for predicates, allowing a pattern to be expressed without permanently tying it to the source domain's vocabulary. The algorithm then instantiates these formulas using predicates from the target domain.

The authors report successful knowledge transfer between molecular biology, social network, and Web domains. Discovered patterns include symmetry, transitivity, and forms of homophily, which concern how relations behave or interact. These findings illustrate why relational structure can be useful across domains with different descriptions. The transferable knowledge is expressed as a reusable pattern among predicates, enabling the target domain to supply its own concrete relations.
icml-2009-deep-transfer-via-second-order.tldr: Second-order Markov logic transfers relational patterns across domains by replacing source predicates with target predicates in learned formulas.

paragraphs: When several source domains have labeled data, each can supply a trained classifier. The challenge is to use those classifiers to predict labels in a different target domain. This paper introduces Domain Adaptation Machine, or DAM, which learns a target decision function from a collection of independently trained source classifiers.

DAM adds a data-dependent regularizer to a least-squares support vector machine. Based on a smoothness assumption, this term encourages the target classifier to produce decision values similar to those of relevant source classifiers on unlabeled target examples. Those target examples therefore help connect existing source predictions to the classifier being learned. A separate sparsity regularizer encourages a sparse target classifier.

Experiments on the TRECVID 2005 corpus evaluate the method for video concept detection. The authors report better effectiveness and efficiency than existing multiple-source adaptation methods in this evaluation. The approach matters because it uses the behavior of available classifiers on target data to guide adaptation, bringing source knowledge and target-domain observations into the same training objective.
icml-2009-domain-adaptation-from-multipl.tldr: DAM adapts multiple source classifiers through agreement on unlabeled target data and reports improved video concept detection effectiveness and efficiency.

paragraphs: Transfer learning uses auxiliary data to help with a target prediction task. EigenTransfer proposes a common framework for several forms of this problem. Its starting point is a graph representing the transfer task, allowing the structure relevant to that task to be expressed before choosing the final classifier.

The framework learns spectral information from the graph and obtains eigenvectors reflecting its intrinsic structure. These eigenvectors become new features through which auxiliary knowledge can help classify target data. A conventional learner, such as a support vector machine, can then operate on the resulting representation. This gives the framework a way to turn a non-transfer learner into a learner suited to a particular transfer task.

The authors apply EigenTransfer to cross-domain, cross-category, and self-taught learning, demonstrating the breadth of the construction. Experiments show that it can substantially outperform several representative non-transfer learners. The reported results support the usefulness of graph-derived representations in these settings, while the unifying contribution is the same feature-construction strategy across different kinds of transfer.
icml-2009-eigentransfer-a-unified-framew.tldr: EigenTransfer converts graph eigenvectors into features that let conventional classifiers use auxiliary knowledge across several transfer-learning settings.

paragraphs: Multiresolution models describe variables at several levels of detail. In the Gaussian models considered here, hidden variables at coarser scales capture dependencies among the finest-scale variables. A tree connecting the scales provides useful structure, but it imposes a restriction: variables within a scale become independent once the other scales are given.

The paper introduces a class of models that can represent correlations left over within each scale. It uses sparse conditional covariance structure to capture these residual relationships. The learning goal has two parts: discover a tree connecting variables across scales and learn the sparse within-scale covariance structure conditional on the other scales.

This combination expands what the model can express while retaining structure that supports efficient computation. The authors derive a new inference algorithm with similarities to multipole methods from computational physics. The contribution is a way to accommodate both broad dependencies across levels and remaining associations within a level, without forcing the cross-scale tree to account for every statistical relationship.
icml-2009-exploiting-sparse-markov-and-c.tldr: The paper combines cross-scale trees with sparse within-scale covariances to make Gaussian multiresolution models more expressive while supporting efficient inference.

paragraphs: A collection of vectors describes data through numerical coordinates, while a graph describes connections. This paper introduces a measure of how well a graph fits vector data. The measure turns graph construction into an optimization task, giving a concrete criterion for selecting a graph that represents the collection.

Optimal graphs under this criterion can be computed using convex quadratic programs. They also satisfy structural guarantees tied to the dimension of the vectors. For data in d dimensions, average degree is at most 2(d+1). For two-dimensional vectors, the optimal graphs are always planar. These properties describe the graphs produced by this particular fitting criterion.

The authors compute the graphs for many standard datasets and show that they can support good solutions to classification, regression, and clustering problems. This connects the graph-fitting objective to several different learning uses. The contribution combines a computable measure of fit, mathematical restrictions on the resulting graphs, and empirical evidence that the connections found can be useful for prediction and grouping.
icml-2009-fitting-a-graph-to-vector-data.tldr: A convex graph-fitting criterion produces graphs with dimension-dependent structural guarantees and useful results across several learning tasks.

paragraphs: Supervised learning usually relies on provided labels, but the people or systems supplying them can differ in quality. This paper considers a heterogeneous set of teachers, including weak, incompetent, and potentially malicious labelers. The learning problem includes coping with unreliable supervision as well as fitting a classifier.

The main algorithm builds on the support vector machine framework and explicitly tries to reduce the influence of low-quality or malicious teachers. It does so without receiving prior information about their reliability. It also avoids requiring multiple teachers to label the same example, so repeated annotation is not part of its information requirements.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis and empirical evidence for the main algorithm. They also introduce a second algorithm with promising experimental results but no formal analysis. These are different levels of support for the two proposals. Together, the methods explore how a learner can account for uneven teacher quality during training, instead of giving every source of labels the same influence by default.
icml-2009-good-learners-for-evil-teacher.tldr: An SVM-based learner reduces unreliable teachers' influence without prior reliability information or repeated labeling of examples.

paragraphs: Training continuous-density hidden Markov models with only partially labeled states creates a difficult large-margin optimization problem. This setting occurs in speech and handwriting recognition, where the available labels do not fully specify the underlying states. The abstract identifies nonconvexity as the obstacle that has led earlier approaches to use severe approximations.

The paper proposes an algorithm based on nonconvex optimization and bundle methods. Its purpose is to tackle the original training objective directly, preserving the problem that the large-margin formulation asks the learner to solve. This makes the optimization method itself the central contribution to learning from partially observed sequences.

The authors prove convergence to a solution with accuracy epsilon at a rate of O(1/epsilon). The abstract does not characterize this as a guarantee of global optimality, so the convergence result should retain that distinction. Experiments in speech recognition and handwriting recognition demonstrate the method's potential. Together, the theory and evaluations support addressing the original nonconvex objective with a dedicated algorithm.
icml-2009-large-margin-training-for-hidd.tldr: A nonconvex bundle-method algorithm directly trains partially labeled hidden Markov models and has a stated O(1/epsilon) convergence rate.

paragraphs: The paper asks which sounds are present in a mixed audio signal. It focuses on situations where only a small, unknown subset of many possible sources overlaps at a given time. This motivates representing the observed signal as a linear combination of a few active sources, using a sparse form of regularized linear regression.

Individual sources are represented by autoregressive models of their waveforms. These models capture acoustic variability, and their coefficients must be learned from examples when the sources are not already known. Learning the dictionary therefore involves learning dynamical descriptions of sounds, as well as deciding which descriptions explain a mixture.

A central technical contribution concerns dynamical stability. The authors show how to estimate stable autoregressive models by replacing a difficult eigenvalue problem with a simple convex optimization problem. They demonstrate the overall approach by learning dictionaries of musical notes and analyzing polyphonic piano, cello, and violin recordings. The method connects sparse source identification with a tractable way to learn stable models of the individual sounds.
icml-2009-learning-dictionaries-of-stabl.tldr: The method identifies overlapping sounds with sparse regression and learns stable autoregressive sound dictionaries through convex optimization.

paragraphs: Practical similarity measures do not always produce matrices suitable for standard kernel methods. In particular, an indefinite similarity matrix can make the associated optimization nonconvex. This paper studies how to classify data using such similarities while recovering a formulation that supports convex optimization.

The proposed method jointly seeks a reproducing kernel Hilbert space based on the supplied similarities and a classifier intended to generalize well within that space. The representation and prediction problem are therefore addressed together. The authors formulate this joint task as a convex optimization problem, providing a route from indefinite similarities to kernel-based classification.

They also develop a simplified version that can reduce overfitting. Its optimization is a convex conic program whose special structure allows very efficient solution. The paper compares the proposed methods with five alternatives on real datasets. The abstract specifies that comparison without claiming a particular ranking of results. The main contribution is the joint convex formulation and its simpler variant, which make otherwise problematic similarity information usable for learning.
icml-2009-learning-kernels-from-indefini.tldr: A convex formulation jointly learns a valid kernel space and classifier from indefinite similarities, with an efficient simplified variant.

paragraphs: Training an image segmenter requires images with regions labeled, and choosing which images to annotate can affect how much supervision is needed. This paper studies active selection from a large pool of unsegmented images, assuming access to an oracle that can supply a segmentation for any selected image.

The learner trains a discriminative random field and chooses images according to their expected information value. It first selects the image whose anticipated labeling would most reduce uncertainty about the remaining unlabeled images. It then continues with greedy selection of the most informative image from the pool. The selection process is aimed at accuracy over the image distribution.

Experiments cover brain tumor segmentation in magnetic resonance images and sky segmentation in ordinary images. In these evaluations, training on very few informative images, in some cases as few as two, can match training on the entire dataset. This is an empirical finding for the studied settings. It illustrates how carefully chosen annotations can supply much of the useful supervision contained in a larger labeled collection.
icml-2009-learning-to-segment-from-a-few.tldr: Active image selection sometimes matched full-dataset segmentation training with as few as two annotated images in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Continuous-density hidden Markov models used in speech recognition often describe emissions with Gaussian distributions or mixtures of Gaussians. These are commonly parameterized by means and covariance matrices. This paper changes that representation to support a simple, mistake-driven approach to discriminative training.

The authors encode the Gaussian mean and covariance information together in positive semidefinite matrices. They then develop perceptron-style updates within the resulting parameter space. The updates seek to reduce the distance between the transcription produced by Viterbi decoding and the target transcription, connecting parameter changes directly to decoding mistakes.

Experiments use context-independent models trained on the TIMIT speech corpus. The study compares different update forms, matrix factorizations, initialization choices, and averaging schemes, examining phone accuracy and convergence rates. Certain forms of perceptron training produce consistently significant and rapid reductions in phone error. The qualification matters because the finding concerns particular training choices. The contribution shows how a matrix representation of Gaussian emissions can enable effective mistake-driven learning for these sequence models.
icml-2009-matrix-updates-for-perceptron-.tldr: Matrix-based Gaussian parameterizations enable perceptron training that rapidly reduces phone errors for certain hidden Markov model update schemes.

paragraphs: Clustering high-dimensional data often begins by projecting it into fewer dimensions. This paper considers how multiple views of the same data can guide that projection. It uses canonical correlation analysis, or CCA, to construct a lower-dimensional representation from the relationships between views before clustering.

The theoretical results assume that the views are uncorrelated once the cluster label is given. Under this assumption, the algorithm succeeds under significantly weaker separation conditions than those in prior results. The authors establish results for mixtures of Gaussian distributions and mixtures of log-concave distributions. The assumption is central to the claimed improvement in required cluster separation.

Empirical support comes from two settings with naturally different views. Audio-visual speaker clustering aims to group observations by speaker identity. Hierarchical Wikipedia clustering uses document words as one view and link structure as another. These examples connect the theory to data with complementary descriptions. The paper's contribution is to show how cross-view information can support useful projections and, under the stated condition, improve clustering guarantees.
icml-2009-multi-view-clustering-via-cano.tldr: CCA-based projections yield weaker sufficient cluster-separation requirements when views are uncorrelated conditional on the cluster label.

paragraphs: A precision-recall curve summarizes how a scoring function distinguishes two populations as its decision threshold changes. The curve computed from a dataset is an estimate, so its reliability depends on sampling variation. This paper studies both the mathematical behavior of that estimate and practical ways to express uncertainty around it.

The authors establish consistency and asymptotic normality for the empirical precision-recall curve in the supremum norm. This addresses deviations across the curve rather than evaluating only an isolated threshold. Consistency concerns the estimate approaching the underlying curve, while asymptotic normality describes its large-sample fluctuations.

The paper also considers confidence bands in precision-recall space. It promotes a bootstrap procedure based on a smoothed and truncated version of the empirical data distribution. The authors give theoretical and computational arguments for preferring this resampling procedure to a naive bootstrap in this setting. The contribution makes uncertainty around an estimated curve a statistical object to analyze, complementing the usual visual comparison of scoring functions.
icml-2009-nonparametric-estimation-of-th.tldr: The paper establishes statistical guarantees for empirical precision-recall curves and proposes a modified bootstrap for confidence bands.

paragraphs: Many optimization guarantees depend on an objective having enough curvature, especially strong convexity. Yet the regularization choice that gives the best test performance may leave a learning objective nearly flat or without that curvature. This creates tension between the statistical choice of objective and the requirements of an efficient training algorithm.

The paper introduces online and batch algorithms based on proximal regularization. They solve the original problem through a sequence of modified optimization tasks whose objectives have greater curvature. This supplies useful optimization structure along the way while retaining the original learning problem as the goal. The approach applies to models including SVMs, logistic regression, structured predictors, and conditional random fields.

The theoretical results provide low regret in online learning and fast convergence in batch learning. Experiments on medium- and large-scale SVM and structured learning tasks report improvements over methods including Pegasos and bundle methods. These results support proximal regularization as a way to train effectively when the preferred regularization setting does not itself provide much curvature.
icml-2009-proximal-regularization-for-on.tldr: Proximal regularization enables efficient online and batch training when the preferred learning objective has little or no curvature.

paragraphs: Selective sampling lets a classifier decide which incoming examples need labels. This paper proposes a binary classification algorithm using regularized least squares, which also supports efficient operation in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The key question is how to request labels while retaining meaningful performance guarantees.

Its sampling rule uses a simultaneous upper bound on the estimator's bias and variance under a simple linear label-noise model. This supports guarantees for an arbitrary sequence of instances, rather than requiring the instances to be independently sampled. The noise-model assumption remains part of the setting in which the analysis applies.

The strategy approximates the Bayes-optimal classifier's margin to accuracy epsilon using roughly d/epsilon squared label queries, with logarithmic factors suppressed. In kernel spaces, a suitable spectral quantity replaces d. This improves the previous bound of roughly d cubed/epsilon to the fourth in the same harder setting, matching standard rates from fully supervised independent sampling. Preliminary experiments also show good practical performance for some of the proposed algorithms.
icml-2009-robust-bounds-for-classificati.tldr: Bias-and-variance-based label selection improves query bounds for arbitrary instance sequences under a linear label-noise model.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian network's structure means selecting relationships among variables from data and any available expert knowledge. This paper studies exact structure learning with decomposable scoring functions. It first identifies properties that reduce time and memory requirements for several search approaches, including hill-climbing, dynamic programming, and sampling variable orderings.

The authors then present a branch-and-bound algorithm that combines data with constraints on both parameters and structure. It guarantees global optimality with respect to the score function. It is also an anytime procedure: if interrupted, it returns the best solution found so far and an estimate of its distance from the global solution.

Experiments demonstrate benefits from the proposed properties and constraints. They also show applicability to datasets with up to one hundred variables, compared with the roughly thirty-variable limit described for other contemporary methods. This is an empirical scalability result, not a guarantee for every problem of that size. The combination of constraints, search reductions, and an optimality-gap estimate makes exact learning more usable when full search is expensive.
icml-2009-structure-learning-of-bayesian.tldr: Constraint-aware branch-and-bound supports exact Bayesian network structure learning and returns a current solution with a gap estimate if interrupted.

paragraphs: This paper connects a probabilistic learning problem to structure learning and feature selection in reinforcement learning. It first formalizes the problem within the KWIK framework and studies the Adaptive k-Meteorologists Algorithm. This establishes a learning component that can then be used inside broader reinforcement-learning procedures.

The authors analyze an upper bound on the algorithm's sample complexity and provide a matching lower bound. The paired bounds give both an achievable requirement and a corresponding limit for the studied problem. They then use the algorithm to construct a reinforcement-learning method for factored-state problems, reporting a significant improvement over the previous state-of-the-art algorithm.

A further application removes a limiting assumption from an existing reinforcement-learning algorithm. The abstract does not identify that assumption, so the supported conclusion is that the method broadens that algorithm's applicability. Experiments in benchmark domains and a robotics navigation problem demonstrate the effectiveness of the approaches. The overall contribution links a theoretically characterized probabilistic learner to two concrete improvements in reinforcement learning.
icml-2009-the-adaptive-k-meteorologists-.tldr: The Adaptive k-Meteorologists Algorithm has matching sample-complexity bounds and enables improvements to factored-state reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs with internal organization, such as a parse, rather than a single class label. This paper adapts the search-based structured prediction algorithm Searn to unsupervised learning. The challenge is to learn useful structured outputs when the desired structures are not supplied as training labels.

The key ingredient is an application of the predict-self idea, which enables the authors to reduce an unsupervised learning problem to supervised learning. This provides a way to use supervised learning machinery within an unsupervised procedure. The paper also establishes a close connection between unsupervised Searn and expectation maximization, relating the new construction to another approach to learning with unobserved structure.

The authors demonstrate a high-quality unsupervised shift-reduce parsing model and show the effectiveness of a semi-supervised extension. These demonstrations give concrete support for the adaptation in parsing and in a setting that also uses supervision. The contribution is both a reduction that makes search-based prediction available for unsupervised learning and an application showing that the resulting method can learn useful structures.
icml-2009-unsupervised-search-based-stru.tldr: An unsupervised adaptation of Searn uses predict-self learning to reduce unsupervised problems to supervised learning and demonstrates effective parsing.
